author: reek
body: THE MIRROR IS ONE WRAPPER AROUND THE WHOLE DISPATCH, not a write at each command. Every command in this console reports by setting `status`, so one echo here covers all of them and cannot fall out of step with a command added later; a write per arm would have to be remembered every time, and the arms that forgot would look exactly like commands that produced no output.

author: reek
body: It echoes the line that arrived as well as the answer. A reader at the far end of COM1 sees only what is written, so without the echo a transcript would be a column of answers to questions it cannot see, and with remote input on there is no keyboard anywhere for them to have been typed at.

author: reek
body: THE FLAG IS READ FROM THE STATE THE COMMAND PRODUCED, not the one it was given, and that is what makes `serial.on` mirror itself. Reading the old state would turn the mirror on and say nothing about it, so the first line of every mirrored session would be missing exactly when someone is checking whether the mirror works.

author: reek
body: THE `before` FLAG IS READ INTO A LOCAL FIRST, AND IT HAS TO BE. `__record-set` mutates the record in place, so the incoming `state` and the returned `after` are the SAME debugger record; reading `state.debugger.serial-mirror` after the route has run reads the value the command just wrote, not the one it started with. Written the obvious way, `serial.off` therefore saw False for both halves and went silent without announcing itself -- the exact ambiguity the `before` flag exists to remove, reintroduced by the aliasing rather than by the logic.

author: reek
body: EITHER FLAG ARMS THE ECHO, the one before the command or the one after, and the `before` half exists entirely so that `serial.off` announces its own switch-off. With only the `after` flag the stream simply stops, and a reader at the far end cannot tell a mirror that was turned off from a console that has hung -- which is the precise question this module was built to answer, so leaving it ambiguous would have hollowed out the feature while every test still passed.

author: reek
body: The `after` half is what makes `serial.on` mirror itself: reading only the incoming state would turn the mirror on and say nothing, so the first line of a session would be missing exactly when someone is checking that the mirror works at all.

author: reek
body: `read` and `write` act at the CURSOR, like `watch`. Both used to set a status saying "enter address" and then consume nothing, so the next line fell through to the evaluator, moved the cursor, and no read or write ever happened -- two menu items the console could not perform. A read answers immediately. A write needs a value, so it is the one command that arms `pending`.

author: reek
body: A line arrives as a value only when a command asked for one. Otherwise it is an address expression, exactly as before.

author: reek
body: `Address Lookup` was in the menu with no arm at all, so the key fell through to the evaluator and answered `expr: unknown name addr`. It needs no argument -- it asks what the cursor is pointing AT -- and `resolve-addr` already existed to answer it.

author: reek
body: A search is a PATTERN at the cursor and a compare is the cursor against ONE other address, so each takes a single line and neither needs a multi-argument parser. The window in both cases is the dump length, which is the same rule `watch` uses: the region acted on is the region `mem` would have shown.

author: reek
body: A PORT NUMBER IS AN EXPRESSION SEEDED WITH ZERO, not with a cursor. The disk prompts seed `$` with the disk cursor and the CPUID prompt with the leaf cursor, each because a number from another space is meaningless in theirs. A port is a sixth such space, and the argument that earned those cursors does not carry here: nobody steps through the I/O map, they type the port the manual names. Seeding zero keeps `$` defined and makes it mean nothing in particular, which is what it is.

author: reek
body: Arming and clearing are the whole of the trace's control surface. There is no per-port filter: the ring holds sixty-four entries and a filter would be a second thing to get right for a report an operator can read in one screen.

author: reek
body: The disk commands take the same shape as the memory ones: an expression supplies the sector, the command acts there, and one argument is enough. A dump is a sector; a compare is the disk cursor against one other sector. `disk.sb`, `disk.facts` and `disk.sc` take no argument at all, because they ask about the store and the medium rather than about a place the operator chose.

author: reek
body: `$` MEANS THE DISK CURSOR IN THESE PROMPTS, not the memory cursor. A prompt that has just asked for an LBA and then read `$` as a physical address would answer with a sector number six orders of magnitude away from anything on the medium. So the evaluator is seeded with `last-lba` here and `last-address` everywhere else, and `$ + 1` means the next sector, which is what a person stepping through a disk means by it.

author: reek
body: The multi-line reports go to `disk-lines` and switch the view, rather than into the one-line status. The sector is read once, here, for the reason given in `DevDebugger`: a view that read it would re-read on every repaint.

author: reek
body: The three interrupt reports that need no argument share one function, because they differ only in which list they render. The disk commands could not: each of those performs I/O and has its own effect row, so there was nothing to share.

author: reek
body: The vector is an EXPRESSION seeded with `last-vector`, the same rule the rest of this console follows, so `$ + 1` steps to the next gate. The seed is the vector cursor and not `last-address`: an address seeded here would make `$ + 1` mean a vector six orders of magnitude outside the table, which `ii-entry-report` would then correctly refuse and the operator would read as the command being broken.

author: reek
body: THE CURSOR MOVES ONLY WHEN THE VECTOR WAS ACCEPTED. A refused vector leaves `last-vector` where it was, so the next `$` still means the last gate actually looked at rather than the out-of-range number just typed.

author: reek
body: The status line names the new state rather than acknowledging the command, so a mirrored session shows what the flag IS at the moment it changed, which is what a reader at the far end needs.

author: reek
body: A macro needs TWO lines, which no other command here does, so the name arrives first and is parked in `macro-name` while the body is asked for. Neither line is an expression: a macro name is a name, and a body is a list of command keys, so both bypass `ExprEval` for the reason `sym` and `bp-add` do.

author: reek
body: THE NESTING REFUSAL IS HERE AND IT IS THE ONLY BOUND ON RECURSION. A body containing `macro.run` would otherwise reach this function again, and a macro that names itself would not stop. There is no fuel and no depth count: while one macro is running, another is refused outright, which is one flag to read rather than a limit to get right and then trust.

author: reek
body: The commands run through `handle-console-input`, which is the same door a typed line comes through, so a macro can do exactly what an operator can and nothing else. It also means each step MIRRORS when the serial mirror is on, and a reader at the far end sees the macro's steps rather than one unexplained final status.

author: reek
body: The flag is cleared on the way out, and leaving it set would refuse every macro for the rest of the session -- a worse defect than the nesting it prevents, and one a test that checked only the refusal would miss.

author: reek
body: THE SUMMARY CARRIES THE LAST COMMAND'S STATUS RATHER THAN REPLACING IT. A macro's own summary reads the same whether every step succeeded or the third was refused, so a summary alone makes an in-macro refusal invisible on screen -- the nesting refusal in particular, which is the one an operator most needs to see. Both are reported: the summary says what ran, the tail says where it ended.

author: reek
body: The status is read into a local BEFORE the debugger record is written, because `__record-set` mutates in place and the two are the same record.

author: reek
body: A repeat reuses the macro runner by building the command list, so the count bound and the one-command-at-a-time execution are the same code rather than a second copy that could drift from it.

author: reek
body: `cpu.cr` and `cpu.feat` need no argument and go straight to the report. `cpu.cpuid` needs a leaf, and takes it the way every other argument in this console is taken: an expression, seeded from its own cursor, so `$ + 1` walks to the next leaf.

author: reek
body: THE CURSOR MOVES ONLY ON A LEAF THE PROCESSOR ACCEPTED, the same rule the IDT vector follows. A refused leaf leaving the cursor behind would make the next `$` mean a leaf that does not exist, so a second `$ + 1` would walk further into nothing rather than back to solid ground.

author: reek
body: `sym` and `bp-add` are the two commands whose argument is a NAME, and both had working implementations with no caller: `debug-sym-lookup` and `bp-add-symbolic` were defined here and reached from nowhere, while the menu offered both. The line each prompted for went to the address evaluator and moved the cursor.

author: reek
body: Neither name goes through `ExprEval`, and that is the point of the variant. A name is not an expression; handing `main` to an evaluator answers "unknown name" for something that was never one.

author: reek
body: `bp-add-symbolic` reports through the DEBUGGER's status field and this console draws the CONSOLE's, so the answer is copied across. Two status fields is not a shape worth defending, but collapsing them is a wider change than this one and would touch every debug command.

author: reek
body: THE PENDING FLAG IS CLEARED BEFORE THE EXPRESSION IS EVALUATED, on both paths. If a bad value left the write armed, the next line the operator typed -- most likely an address expression, since that is what every other line here is -- would be taken as the value and written to memory. A refusal that stays armed is worse than the refusal it reports.

author: reek
body: `$` is the last address, which is the reading a person at a debugger means by it: look at something, then look a little past it.

author: reek
body: A bad expression sets the status to the reason and leaves last-address ALONE. Moving the cursor to a value the evaluator could not compute is how you dump the wrong page and believe it.

author: reek
body: The length is the dump length, so the region you watch is the region `mem` would show you. Two different defaults would be two numbers to keep straight for no reason.

author: reek
body: The check writes the re-armed table back. Dropping it would leave every watch reporting its first change forever, which is the defect `dev-watch-check` is written against and which its own test ablates.

author: reek
body: Compile-and-run needs a guest to run the compiler in, and that guest is a VMX one. So the first thing this asks is whether this machine can enter VMX operation at all, and it says so plainly when it cannot -- naming the MSR and what to do about it -- rather than reporting "(pending)", which was true of the feature and told an operator nothing about their machine.

author: reek
body: The honest state, stated once here so it is not discovered twice: on a machine with VT-x the run path is `vm-compile-cdx` then `vm-run-cdx`, and it is **unexercised**, because no emulator this project tests under exposes nested VMX. What IS exercised, and every battery run exercises it, is the refusal: `codex/test/apps/vmx-init-test` requires this machine to be told the truth about itself.

author: reek
body: The install lives in `Kernel chapter DriveManager` and this is the menu entry for it. It used to be a second copy of the whole sequence, and the copy read the SOURCE volume's boot sector while the TARGET was still selected -- one line before it selected the source. That was unreachable while block-select did nothing, and became a real wrong read the moment it started working.
